title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of producing legal answers, memos, and briefs where every claim is tied to a retrieved primary or secondary source, such as a case, statute, regulation, or treatise. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of producing legal answers, memos, and briefs where every claim is tied to a retrieved primary or secondary source, such as a case, statute, regulation, or treatise. It covers state and federal law, court rules, agency guidance, and practice commentary. The method is used for issue spotting, case strategy, and due diligence, and it differs from open-ended chatbot output by requiring a citation for each proposition. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents, which are among the sources a retrieval-grounded system can draw on.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: It runs on indexed collections of legal text, including court opinions, statutes, regulations, and law review articles, stored in databases that support both keyword and semantic search. A retriever selects relevant passages, and a language model generates an answer from those passages rather than from memory alone. Commercial platforms such as Westlaw and LexisNexis provide proprietary headnotes and citators, while open sources like CourtListener and state legislature websites supply raw documents. The site's 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6825 state AI bills are examples of source corpora that can be loaded into such a system.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A lawyer or paralegal enters a research question, and the system first retrieves a set of candidate passages by lexical matching, vector similarity, or a combination of both. The language model then drafts an answer that quotes or paraphrases only the retrieved text, and each sentence is linked to its source. A citation checker verifies that the cited page or paragraph actually supports the statement, and any unsupported claim is removed or flagged for review. The attorney then reads the underlying authorities to confirm jurisdiction, currency, and contrary holdings before relying on the output.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are hallucinated citations, reliance on overturned or superseded law, and failure to surface adverse authority that a keyword search missed. Provenance is handled by requiring a pinpoint citation for every factual or legal assertion, and by logging which version of a document was retrieved. In the United States, court opinions and statutes are generally not copyrightable, but proprietary headnotes, annotations, and citator signals are, so a system must separate public domain text from licensed content. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shape how courts treat AI-generated legal work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is moving toward real-time ingestion of new filings, docket entries, and legislative changes, so that answers reflect the law as of the moment of query. Systems are beginning to compare multiple jurisdictions side by side and to flag conflicts between authorities automatically. The site's 6825 state AI bills indicate a fast-changing statutory landscape that retrieval systems will need to track daily. Future tools may integrate with e-discovery and contract review, and produce court-ready documents with an auditable chain from each sentence to its source.
